summary: Describes how the DetNet IP data plane can support Packet Replication, Elimination, and Ordering Functions (PREOF). It builds on the existing PREOF solution for the DetNet MPLS data plane and on MPLS-over-UDP technology.

eli5.summary: To make sure an important letter arrives, you send copies by different roads and throw away extras. This explains how to do that over ordinary internet packets.

subtitle: Reliable message delivery over IP using replication, elimination and ordering

tldr.problem: Deterministic networks need to reliably deliver critical packets. DetNet MPLS supports packet replication and redundancy, but the DetNet IP data plane did not have a standard way to add these protections.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC adds support for PREOF (Packet Replication, Elimination, and Ordering Functions) to DetNet IP by combining MPLS-over-UDP/IP encapsulation with DetNet sequencing information, enabling redundant paths without requiring an MPLS forwarding plane.
tldr.outcome: DetNet IP networks can now provide end-to-end service protection through replication and elimination of duplicate packets, matching the reliability offered by DetNet MPLS.

facts.label: Routing layer
facts.value: DetNet forwarding sub-layer with UDP tunnel

today: RFC 9566 is an Informational document with IETF community consensus. It has not been obsoleted or updated. DetNet PREOF over UDP/IP is now a defined standard way to add redundancy and ordering protections to IP-based deterministic networks.

sections.title: Introduction to DetNet PREOF
sections.content:
DetNet (Deterministic Networking) specifies how to deliver critical packets across networks with guaranteed timing and no loss. DetNet defines three protection functions: Packet Replication (PRF) creates multiple copies of a packet, Packet Elimination (PEF) removes duplicate copies, and Packet Ordering (POF) reorders out-of-sequence packets.

The DetNet MPLS data plane already supports PREOF, but the DetNet IP data plane (which sends data directly over UDP and IP) did not have a standard way to include the sequencing information that PREOF needs. This RFC solves that by reusing the DetNet MPLS-over-UDP/IP encapsulation technology, allowing DetNet IP to gain the same protection capabilities.
sections.eli5: Some networks need to guarantee messages arrive on time without loss. DetNet is the IETF way to do that. This describes how to add copy-and-discard redundancy to regular IP networks.

sections.title: The Three Protection Functions
sections.content:
Packet Replication (PRF) sends multiple copies of the same packet over different, maximally disjoint paths. This ensures that if one copy is lost due to a network failure, other copies may arrive.

Packet Elimination (PEF) receives multiple copies of the same packet and uses sequence numbers to identify and remove duplicates, passing only one copy to the destination. Without elimination, the receiving application would see duplicate packets.

Packet Ordering (POF) takes packets that arrive out of order and reorders them based on their sequence numbers, so they are delivered to the application in the correct sequence.

Together, these functions provide service protection: the network guarantees that each original packet reaches the destination exactly once, in order, even if components fail or packets are lost in transit.
sections.eli5: Send copies (replication) means you make extra copies. Remove doubles (elimination) means you trash the extra ones that arrived. Put in order (ordering) means you arrange them the right way. Together they mean: reliable delivery.

sections.title: Solution Design: Combining MPLS and UDP
sections.content:
The solution reuses the DetNet MPLS-over-UDP/IP encapsulation defined in RFC 9025, but restricts it to use zero F-Labels (Forwarding labels). The encapsulation works as follows:

At the DetNet service sub-layer, each packet gets a DetNet Control Word (d-CW) that carries the sequence number needed by PREOF, and a Service-ID (S-Label) that identifies which DetNet flow the packet belongs to. These are placed inside the UDP/IP tunnel, which is handled by the DetNet forwarding sub-layer. This design maintains compatibility with the existing DetNet IP data plane (RFC 8939) while adding PREOF support.

The key insight is that the UDP tunnel handles resource allocation and explicit routing at the forwarding layer, while the Service-ID and Control Word handle PREOF operations at the service layer. This separation lets DetNet IP systems add PREOF with minimal implementation effort.
sections.eli5: You wrap the packet in layers: the sequence number goes in a special header, the flow identity goes in a label, then UDP and IP on the outside. The UDP tunnel carries it across the network; the sequence number tells the receiver what to do with duplicates.

sections.title: Encapsulation and Packet Processing
sections.content:
The encapsulation adds three layers to the original DetNet application packet: a DetNet Control Word with sequence information, a Service-ID, and a UDP/IP header. A PREOF-capable DetNet IP domain can use multiple member flows (copies) of the same packet, each with its own Service-ID, UDP source port, and routing information.

At ingress, the service sub-layer adds these headers and the sequence number. At transit nodes, the UDP tunnel carries the packet to the next DetNet node. At egress, the service sub-layer uses the sequence number in the Control Word to eliminate duplicates (via PEF), reorder packets (via POF), or both.

Service-ID values are receiver-driven: the receiving node assigns them to identify incoming flows, not the sending node. This allows a single replication node to send copies to multiple elimination nodes, each with different Service-ID values.
sections.eli5: You tag each packet with a sequence number and a label saying which flow it belongs to, wrap it in UDP and IP, and send it. At the other end, the receiver uses the sequence number to throw away duplicates and put things in order.

sections.title: Flow Aggregation and Configuration
sections.content:
DetNet supports two methods of flow aggregation. The first method puts multiple DetNet flows in the same UDP tunnel; they are treated as one flow at the forwarding layer but use different Service-IDs at the service layer. The second method creates a hierarchy by adding a second Service-ID and Control Word pair, forming an Aggregate-ID.

Configuration of DetNet flows and aggregation is done via a control plane (such as a network controller) and includes parameters like IPv4/IPv6 addresses, port ranges, DSCP values, and maximum packet sizes. The DetNet service sub-layer must know which PREOF operations to apply (replication, elimination, ordering) and the UDP tunnel must be configured with resource allocation and explicit paths to handle the expected traffic.
sections.eli5: You can put several flows through the same UDP tunnel if they follow the same path, or you can nest them by adding extra labels. A network controller tells each node what to do with each flow.
